facts.value: Treasury Management Strategy Outturn 2025/26. Report to Audit and Performance Committee, 30 June 2026, onward to Full Council by 30 September 2026 (regulatory requirement, para 1.2). Signed by Gerald Almeroth, Executive Director for Finance and Resources; report author Sophie Green, Treasury Manager (contact sgreen1@westminster.gov.uk, page 11 background papers block).

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy Outturn 2025/26 — Audit and Performance Committee, 30 June 2026

facts.note: Twelve-page outturn covering the full 2025/26 year, plus Appendix 1 (page 12) listing counterparty limits and exposures at 31/3/26. Report says the Council complied with all elements of the TMSS (para 1.5). Treasury operation is run by the Tri-Borough Treasury team (para 3.1).

facts.value: 31/3/26: Total Borrowing £569.0m; Total Cash Invested £306.3m; Net Cash Invested (£262.6m). Comparators 31/3/25: £572.7m borrowing / £463.4m investments / (£109.3m) net. Investment book down £157.1m year on year; borrowing down £3.7m.
facts.note: Para 3.2 states the net-cash position moved £153.3m year on year (from (£109.3m) to (£262.6m)) driven by continued use of internal borrowing to fund capital (paras 3.5, 3.14). Average investable balance across the year £643.6m (para 3.4).

facts.value: 31/3/26 breakdown (para 3.22, page 5): PWLB £113.6m (from £120.7m, −£7.0m); LOBO £40.0m (unchanged); Private Placement £386.4m (from £392.2m, −£5.8m); Amber MEEF/Abundance £28.9m (from £19.8m, +£9.1m). Total £569.0m. GF/HRA split (para 3.21): GF £430.3m (from £427.0m); HRA £138.6m (from £145.7m).
facts.note: PWLB is only 20.0% of the book, LOBOs 7.0%, Private Placements 67.9%, Amber MEEF/Abundance 5.1%. £9.1m of net new borrowing in year via the Amber MEEF/Abundance line — the only rising component. No new PWLB or LOBO borrowing. Para 3.24: council took no additional long-term borrowing in 2025/26 due to high cash holdings, so the £7m PWLB drop is amortisation/maturity and the £5.8m private placement drop is annuity/EIP repayment on the Phoenix and Rothesay tranches.

facts.value: Para 3.26–3.27, page 5: £400m of forward borrowing arranged in 2019/20 with insurance-company counterparties, £386.4m still outstanding at 31/3/26 at a weighted 2.579% average interest rate. Breakdown: Phoenix Group £37.5m initial / £12.8m outstanding at 2.706%, annuity, drawn 15/3/2022, maturing 15/3/2062; Barings LLC £150.0m / £150.0m at 1.970%, maturity, drawn 15/8/2022, maturing 15/8/2052; Phoenix Group £12.5m / £12.0m at 2.751%, annuity, drawn 15/3/2023, maturing 15/3/2063; Rothesay Life Plc £200.0m / £189.0m at 2.887%, equal instalment of principal, drawn 8/5/2023, maturing 8/5/2063.
facts.note: This is the distinctive feature of Westminster's book. Rates locked in 2019/20 for 30–40 year terms at 1.97%–2.89% — years before the October 2019 PWLB margin hike and years before the 2022 gilt sell-off. Explicit rationale (para 3.26): eliminating cost of carry, i.e., the difference between loan interest cost and rate of return on cash investments. Against today's PWLB CERTAINTY curve at notice 314/26 PM (as at 2026-08-14) of ~6.27%–6.46% at 25–50y, the £386.4m book at 2.579% carries in the order of 350–400 basis points of value below current comparable cost. Not something the paper computes; visible from the platform's daily curve.

facts.value: TIES EXACTLY. price_book.py 'WESTMINSTER CITY COUNCIL' --as-at 2026-03-31 returns 14 loans outstanding, principal £113,645,000, weighted rate 3.6016%, all MATURITY profile. Paper's para 3.22 table shows PWLB balance at 31/3/26 of £113.6m. Both sides agree to the pound.

source.title: price_book.py output vs paper para 3.22, page 5

facts.note: Paper prints only the PWLB total, not a PWLB-only weighted rate — its 2.87% overall rate (para 3.38) is for the whole £569m fixed book (dominated by 2.579% private placement). So the 3.60% weighted rate on our PWLB extract cannot be cross-checked to a printed number, but the balance and the composition (PWLB is 20% of the book, everything else is Private Placement / LOBO / Amber MEEF) match cleanly. PWLB spread across the curve: 1 loan £4m <12m at 3.73%; 1 loan £4m 1–2y at 3.81%; 4 loans £27.7m 2–5y at 3.40%; 5 loans £50m 5–10y at 3.52%; 1 loan £7.945m 10–25y at 3.43%; 2 loans £20m 25y+ at 4.10%. Break-cost curve at notice 314/26 PM shows a net DISCOUNT of £9.20m (8.1% of principal), all 14 loans below par — because PWLB certainty rates today (5.34% at 5y, 5.83% at 10y, 6.27% at 50y) sit above the loans' 3.4%–4.1% coupons. INDICATIVE ONLY; only the DMO can quote.

facts.value:
CFR − external borrowing − other long-term liabilities = internal borrowing.
• Using the paper's headline CFR (para 3.19 and summary table page 7): £1,338m − £569m − £286m = £483m internal borrowing. TIES to the paper's stated £483m under-borrowed position (para 3.20 and summary table).
• Using the detailed CFR reconciliation (page 8, total column): £1,748m closing CFR − £569m − £286m = £893m. DOES NOT TIE to the £483m headline.
The two CFR figures in the paper differ: £1,338m appears in both the summary indicator table (page 7) and paragraph 3.19; £1,748m appears as the total closing CFR in the detailed reconciliation on page 8 (GF £1,338m + HRA £410m). The headline figure is the GF-only column, not the total. Both identity calculations are internally consistent to the pound.

source.title: Paras 3.19–3.20 and summary indicator table, page 7; detailed CFR reconciliation, page 8

facts.value: Para 3.6 table, 31/3/26: Money Market Funds £74.3m at 3.83%; UK Banks £10.0m at 4.37%; Non-UK Banks £25.0m at 4.16%; Local Authorities £197.0m at 4.46%; Total £306.3m at weighted 4.28%. Comparators 31/3/25: MMF £33.4m at 4.55%; UK £50.0m at 4.75%; Non-UK £50.0m at 4.78%; LA £330.0m at 5.34%; Total £463.4m at 5.16%. Every yield down between 60 and 90 basis points on Bank Rate cuts through the year (May, August, December, all 25bp — para 3.7).
facts.note: £197m at 4.46% to other councils is a very large LA lender position — Westminster is on the sell side of the inter-authority market at scale. Appendix 1 (page 12) names the counterparties: Doncaster (2 loans, £40m total at 4.25%), Dundee City (3 loans, £40m at 4.50%–4.90%), North Lanarkshire (6 loans, £50m at 4.05%–4.25%), Stockton-on-Tees (£12m at 4.25%), Surrey County Council (£20m at 4.10% and £10m at 7.50%), Telford and Wrekin (3 loans, £25m at 4.25%–4.30%). Total across the list is £197m. That's the LA row exactly.

facts.value: Para 3.11 table: 2025/26 Budget £27,983k, Actual £29,702k, Variance +£1,719k (favourable). Para 3.11 text conflicts with the table, stating budgeted investment return was £41.5m against actual £29.7m for a £11.8m under-budget outcome.

Summary table page 7, 2025/26 actual vs forecast: Capital expenditure £282m (forecast £579m); CFR £1,338m (forecast £1,594m); Net debt vs CFR £483m under-borrowed (forecast £1,035m); External borrowing £569m; Other Long-Term Liabilities £286m; Gross Debt £855m; Authorised Limit for External Debt £1,641m; Operational Boundary £605m — actual gross debt £855m EXCEEDED (para 3.31). Working Capital Balance £0m. Non-specified investment limit (>364d) £450m — actual £0m (para 3.42). Ratio of financing costs to revenue: GF 12.20% (limit 12.55%); HRA 30.33% (limit 58.42%). Maturity profile actual: 3% <12m (limit 40%), 2% 12–24m (limit 35%), 9% 24m–5y (limit 35%), 16% 5–10y (limit 50%), 70% 10y+ (lower limit 35%).

source.title: Summary indicator table, page 7; maturity structure para 3.36, page 6

facts.note: Operational Boundary breach explained by the A2Dominion lease transaction commencing April 2025 after the TMSS was set in February 2025 — para 3.31–3.32. Council remained comfortably within the £1,641m Authorised Limit. GF financing-cost ratio at 12.20% actual sits 35 basis points below its 12.55% limit — narrowest headroom in the summary table. Maturity profile is heavily long: 70% of borrowing sits 10 years and above, driven by the £386.4m private placement book maturing 2052–2063. Only 3% (about £17m of £569m) reprices in under 12 months.

facts.value: Para 3.38, page 6: 'The average rate on the fixed interest borrowing is 2.87% with an average redemption period of 19 years. This reflects the historical legacy of borrowing taken when rates were lower than current comparable PWLB interest rates.' The paper adds: 'Officers have considered loan refinancing but premia for premature redemptions are prohibitively high, making this option poor value for money.'
facts.note: The 2.87% whole-book rate is dominated by the £386.4m of private placements at 2.579% (68% of the book). PWLB piece at ~3.60% is a smaller weight. LOBO piece at £40m and Amber MEEF at £28.9m sit inside the average too. Premature-repayment premia — for the private placements, yes, they would be very high given today's 30–50y curve at 6.27%–6.46% CERTAINTY, versus their 1.97%–2.89% coupons. For the £113.6m PWLB piece specifically, today's DMO curve puts the book at a discount (14 of 14 below par, net £9.2m under principal), because their PWLB coupons (3.4%–4.1%) sit below today's PWLB replacement rates. So the para 3.38 statement is correct for the whole book but not for the PWLB piece considered alone. NOT the argument for the email.

facts.value: Para 3.39, page 6: £40.0m of Lender Option Borrower Option loans, described as up to 60-year term with periodic rate re-pricing. Paper states rates were 'comparable with loans for similar durations provided by the PWLB'. Paper acknowledges refinancing risk from lender option to redeem, and notes some banks offering premature repayment or conversion to fixed-term loans with officers 'alert to such opportunities as they arise'.

Section 4, pages 8–10 (paper's own narrative): UK CPI 3.5% start of year, peaked 3.8% July–Sept 2025, dipped to 3.0% Jan/Feb 2026, core 3.2% Feb. Bank Rate cuts of 0.25% in May, August, December 2025 taking the headline rate 4.50% → 3.75%. Rate at 3.75% at report date; March MPC vote 9-0 to hold, moderately hawkish tone. 10-year gilt yield 4.23% low late-Feb, spiked to 5.00% on Middle East conflict, ended quarter 4.92% with ~65bp of hikes priced in over the coming year. Gilt yields materially higher in March 2026 than earlier in the year.
facts.note: Paper's rate view (3.75% held through 2026, hike risk if inflation picks up) tracks the paper's own year-end market view. Consistent with Arlingclose-style narrative on other August reports, though the paper does not name a treasury adviser.

officer.body:
Dear Sophie,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on your Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 ahead of it reaching Full Council by the end of September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is compact and well-executed and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A quick cross-check first. We hold 14 PWLB loans for the Council totalling £113,645,000 at 31 March 2026, against the £113.6m in your para 3.22 table. To the pound. Your paper doesn't print a PWLB-only weighted rate — the 2.87% at para 3.38 is the whole £569m fixed book — but the balance and composition match cleanly.

The part of the paper that's genuinely distinctive is your para 3.27 table. Of the 77 councils we've read, Westminster is the only book we've come across built around £400m of forward-placement debt with insurers. Barings at 1.970% out to 2052, Rothesay at 2.887% out to 2063, and Phoenix at 2.706% and 2.751% out to 2062 and 2063 — weighted 2.579% across the £386.4m still outstanding. Against today's PWLB certainty curve at notice 314/26 PM (5.83% at 10 years, 6.38% at 20 years, 6.27% at 50 years), that's on the order of 350 to 400 basis points of value locked in below current comparable cost. Your para 3.26 framing — that these loans 'eliminated the cost of carry' between borrowing rate and cash return — is the specialist reading of what happened, and one that reads the same way six years later. The value was in the year the trades went on and it compounds every year they stay in the ground. It's also why your maturity profile prints 70% at 10 years and above against a 35% lower limit, and only 3% under 12 months — refinancing risk isn't the story here in the way it is for most councils we read.

Where the interesting question does sit is the other side of the balance sheet. £197m out to six other councils at a weighted 4.46% at 31 March, against Bank Rate 3.75% and yields off up to 90 basis points across your investment categories through the year (your para 3.6 versus 31 March 2025) — Westminster's Appendix 1 is one of the fuller sell-side snapshots we've seen of the inter-authority market, and it's the market nobody publishes. Every council sees its own trades and none sees the distribution. Our monthly page at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity aggregates what authorities are actually paying for shorter-dated money; July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers, average 5.02%.

On the PWLB side, pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis prices the 14 loans against the DMO's premature repayment curve daily. Standard caveats: we hold PWLB only (LOBO, private placement and Amber MEEF aren't in our file), we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a settlement figure. The rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds for the day's curve.

On training, four fit the shape of your book. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator, for the PWLB piece. Non-PWLB debt: private placement and insurance-company lending, which is the market where the 2019/20 trades sit. LOBO loans, for the £40m at para 3.39 and the 'alert to opportunities' language. And the Liability benchmark pathway is worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are open to the whole team.

And if any of it turns out to be useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
